name: Teacher's Aide and Paraprofessional Preparation
objectives: Given your state and a school district you want to work for, list the qualifications they ask of a paraprofessional and the official pages that state them, naming the education route, any test and passing score, and the background check
Given practice reading, writing and math questions like those on the ParaPro Assessment, answer the questions and explain each mistake, getting at least 8 of 10 right

lessons.title: Lesson 1: The job, and the rules in your state
lessons.text:
Lesson 1 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: List the qualifications your state and one school district ask of a paraprofessional.
This lesson builds toward: Given your state and a school district you want to work for, you will list the qualifications they ask of a paraprofessional and the official pages that state them, naming the education route, any test and passing score, and the background check.
A paraprofessional works under a teacher. You might help a small group read, help a student with a disability follow the lesson, watch the lunchroom or playground, or prepare materials. The teacher plans and grades; you support. Job titles include teacher's aide, instructional assistant, paraeducator and special education aide.
Federal rules cover aides who help with teaching in schools paid for by Title I, the federal program for schools with many low-income families. Those aides need a high school diploma or equivalent, and one of these: two years of college study, an associate degree or higher, or passing a formal state or local test of reading, writing and math. Many schools use the ParaPro Assessment from ETS as that test.
Each state, and sometimes each district, sets its own rules on top of that. ETS lists a qualifying ParaPro score for each state that uses it; in some states each district sets its own score, and some states use other tests (Rhode Island now accepts only ParaPathways). Almost every school also requires a background check and fingerprints. So always check your own state and district before you pay for a test.
Where to check: your state department of education website, the job posting on the district's website, and the state requirements page on parapro.ets.org.
Step by step:
- Search your state's department of education site for "paraprofessional" or "paraeducator".
- Open a real job posting from a district near you and read the requirements.
- Check parapro.ets.org for your state's test and qualifying score.
- Write down the route you already meet or will use: college credits, a degree, or the test.
- Note the background check and any other steps (health screening, training).
Words to know:
- Paraprofessional: a school worker who helps students learn under a teacher's direction; also called a teacher's aide or paraeducator.
- Title I: a federal program that gives extra money to schools with many students from low-income families.
- ParaPro Assessment: a test from ETS of reading, writing and math skills, and of using them to help in a classroom.
- Qualifying score: the lowest score your state or district accepts.
- Background check: a check of criminal and other records that schools do before hiring.
Official sources:
- 34 CFR 200.58: qualifications for Title I paraprofessionals (Cornell LII)
- ETS ParaPro: state requirements and qualifying scores
- ETS ParaPro: about the test
Try it now: Find one real paraprofessional job posting from a school district near you. Write down: the job title, the education or test it asks for, the background check, and the pay if it is listed. Then find your state on the ETS state requirements page and write down whether it uses the ParaPro.
You can now list what your state and a nearby district ask of a paraprofessional, and show where you checked.

check.q: Which route meets the federal rule for a Title I instructional aide, along with a high school diploma?
check.why: The rule lists two years of college, an associate degree or higher, or a formal state or local test.

check.q: A friend says the ParaPro passing score is the same everywhere. What do you do?
options: Check your state, and your district, on the official pages
Believe it and book the test
Skip the test and apply anyway
Ask the friend to take it for you
check.why: Qualifying scores are set by each state, and in some states by each district.

lessons.title: Lesson 2: ParaPro practice: reading and writing
lessons.text:
Lesson 2 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Answer practice reading and writing questions and explain each mistake.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice reading, writing and math questions like those on the ParaPro Assessment, you will answer the questions and explain each mistake, getting at least 8 of 10 right.
ETS says the ParaPro measures reading, writing and math skills and knowledge, and your ability to use them when helping in a classroom. So some questions ask you to read or write well, and some ask how you would help a student with reading or writing.
Reading questions may ask for the main idea of a passage, a detail, what a word means from the words around it, or what the writer suggests without saying it. Read the question first, then the passage, then go back to find the proof.
Writing questions may ask you to find a mistake in grammar, spelling or punctuation, or to choose the best way to fix a sentence. Classroom questions may ask how to help a student sound out a word or fix a run-on sentence.
ETS offers a free Study Companion and Study Guide with sample questions on its test prep page. Use them; they show the real kind of questions better than any other source.
Step by step:
- Read the question before the passage.
- Find the line in the passage that proves your answer.
- For writing items, read the sentence out loud in your head and listen for what sounds wrong.
- Cross out answers you know are wrong, then choose.
- For every mistake, write one line: why the right answer is right.
Words to know:
- Main idea: what a passage is mostly about.
- Context clues: the words around a new word that help you guess its meaning.
- Run-on sentence: two sentences joined without the right punctuation or joining word.
- Phonics: matching letters to their sounds to read words.
Official sources:
- ETS ParaPro: test prep (Study Companion and Study Guide)
- ETS ParaPro: about the test
Try it now: Practice now. 1) Fix this sentence: "The students was excited, they ran to the window." 2) In "The path was so narrow that two people could not walk side by side," what does narrow mean? 3) Write one sentence on how you would help a child who reads "ship" as "sip". Check: "The students were excited, so they ran to the window" (or use a period); narrow means not wide; point to the "sh" and practice its sound together.
You can now answer practice reading and writing questions, find the proof, and explain your mistakes.

options: Her and me helped the class.
Each of the boys have a book.
The teacher and I set up the tables.
check.why: "The teacher and I" is the subject, and "set up" fits it; the others have subject or verb errors.

check.q: A passage says, "The garden was barren; nothing grew there." What does barren mean?
check.why: The clue "nothing grew there" tells you barren means producing nothing.

lessons.title: Lesson 3: ParaPro practice: math, and your study plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 3 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Answer practice math questions and write a study plan with a test date.
This lesson builds toward: Given practice reading, writing and math questions like those on the ParaPro Assessment, you will answer the questions and explain each mistake, getting at least 8 of 10 right. Given your state and a school district you want to work for, you will list the qualifications they ask of a paraprofessional and the official pages that state them, naming the education route, any test and passing score, and the background check.
Math on the ParaPro covers the basics you would help students with: number sense, adding, subtracting, multiplying and dividing, fractions, decimals and percents, simple measurement, reading charts and graphs, and simple equations. Some questions ask how you would explain a math idea to a child.
Work slowly and show your steps on scrap paper. For word problems: find the question, pull out the numbers, decide the operation, solve, then ask "Does this answer make sense?"
A study plan turns "someday" into a date. Find out how to register (at a test center or at home, where offered), check the fee and ID rules on the official site, pick a test date three to six weeks away, and give each week one focus: reading, writing, math, then a full practice set.
Step by step:
- Read the word problem twice and circle the question.
- Write the numbers you need.
- Choose the operation and solve on paper.
- Check that the answer makes sense.
- Put a test date and weekly study focus on a calendar.
Words to know:
- Fraction: a part of a whole, like 3/4.
- Percent: a number out of 100; 25% means 25 out of 100.
- Equation: a math sentence with an equals sign, like 3 + x = 10.
Official sources:
- ETS ParaPro: how to register
- ETS ParaPro: ID requirements
Try it now: Practice now. 1) 24 students share 6 tables equally. How many per table? 2) What is 3/4 written as a percent? 3) 3 + x = 10; what is x? 4) A class reads 12 pages on Monday and 15 on Tuesday. How many pages in all? Answers: 4, 75%, 7, 27. Then write your study plan: test date, and one focus for each week.
You can now solve basic word problems step by step and set a study plan with a real test date.

check.q: Shirts cost $8 each. A teacher buys 5. What is the total?
What should you do BEFORE paying for the ParaPro?
options: Check that your state or district accepts it and what score it needs
Ask a student to quiz you
check.why: ETS advises confirming your state or local agency accepts the test before you schedule.

lessons.title: Lesson 4: Leading a small group from the teacher's plan
lessons.text:
Lesson 4 of 6 · about 5 minutes
Goal: Lead a short small-group practice activity that follows a teacher's plan.
This lesson builds toward: Given a teacher's lesson plan for a small group, you will lead a short practice activity that follows the plan and gives hints before answers, staying on the teacher's goal and writing a two-line note back to the teacher.
The teacher decides what students learn; you help them practice it. Before the group starts, ask the teacher: What is the goal? What should students be able to do at the end? What help is OK to give?
Give hints before answers. A good order is: wait a few seconds, ask a question that points the way ("What sound does this start with?"), show a similar example, and only then show the answer. This is called scaffolding: you give support, then take it away bit by bit.
Praise effort with exact words ("You checked your work, that is how you caught it"). Keep the group on task with short, clear directions. At the end, write a short note for the teacher: who got it, who struggled and with what.
Step by step:
- Ask the teacher for the goal and what help is allowed.
- Get materials ready before students arrive.
- Explain the task in one or two short sentences.
- Give hints before answers: wait, ask, show an example, then show.
- Write a two-line note for the teacher at the end.
Words to know:
- Lesson plan: the teacher's written plan for what students will learn and how.
- Scaffolding: help that lets a student do a task, then is taken away step by step.
- Wait time: a few seconds of silence after a question so students can think.
Try it now: Here is a sample teacher's plan: "Goal: students add two-digit numbers with regrouping. Group: 4 students, 10 minutes." Write your activity: how you explain it in two sentences, three practice problems, two hints you will give before showing an answer, and a two-line note to the teacher. Use made-up first initials, never real student names.
You can now turn a teacher's plan into a short small-group activity with hints and a note back.

check.q: A student is stuck on a word. What is your FIRST move?
options: Say the word for them right away
Wait, then ask what sound it starts with
check.why: Wait time and a pointing question let the student do the thinking first.

check.q: Who decides what the small group should learn?
check.why: The teacher plans the lesson; the aide helps students practice it.

lessons.title: Lesson 5: Behavior support, special education and privacy
lessons.text:
Lesson 5 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Choose calm, positive steps for a behavior and share student information only with staff who need it.
This lesson builds toward: Given a classroom behavior or privacy scenario, you will choose calm, positive steps and share student information only with staff who need it, following the teacher's and the student's plan.
Behavior is a way students communicate. Stay calm and use a low, steady voice. Remind students of the rule in a positive way ("Walking feet" instead of "Don't run"). Notice and praise students who are doing the right thing. Give choices when you can ("Do you want to start with the red or blue page?"). Follow the teacher's classroom plan, and get the teacher or school staff right away if anyone may get hurt.
Many aides work with students who have an IEP, an Individualized Education Program under the federal special education law (IDEA). The IEP or a behavior plan may say exactly what supports a student gets, like extra time, a quiet break or a picture schedule. Ask the teacher what parts of the plan you carry out, and follow them every time.
Student information is private. FERPA is a federal law that gives parents the right to see their child's education records and some control over who else sees them. As an aide, you share grades, behavior, health or IEP details only with school staff who need them for their work. Never talk about students in the community, post about them online or take photos of them on your phone.
Step by step:
- Stay calm and use a low voice.
- State the rule as what to do, not what not to do.
- Praise students who are following it.
- Follow the teacher's plan and the student's IEP or behavior plan.
- Get help right away if anyone may get hurt.
- Share student details only with staff who need them.
Words to know:
- IEP: Individualized Education Program: a written plan for a student with a disability, under the federal law IDEA.
- IDEA: Individuals with Disabilities Education Act, the federal special education law.
- FERPA: a federal law that protects the privacy of student education records.
- Positive behavior support: teaching and praising the behavior you want, not only reacting to problems.
Official sources:
- US Department of Education: What is FERPA?
- US Department of Education: IDEA
Try it now: Scenario: during reading, a student (call him J.) throws his book and says "This is stupid." His behavior plan says he may take a two-minute break at the calm corner. Write what you say and do, in order. Then write who you would tell about it later, and who you would NOT tell.
You can now respond to behavior calmly and positively, follow a student's plan, and keep student information private.

check.q: Which direction is stated in a positive way?
check.why: It tells the student what to do instead of only what not to do.

check.q: A neighbor at the store asks how a student in your class is doing. You:
options: Share a few details since it is a neighbor
Politely say you can't talk about students
Show them the student's work on your phone
check.why: Student information is private and shared only with school staff who need it.

lessons.title: Lesson 6: Keeping children safe and reporting concerns
lessons.text:
Lesson 6 of 6 · about 6 minutes
Goal: Describe the steps you take when you think a child may be harmed, and who you tell.
This lesson builds toward: Given a scenario where a child may be harmed or in danger, you will describe the steps you take, who you tell and when, reporting the same day the way your state and school require, without investigating yourself. Given your state and a school district you want to work for, you will list the qualifications they ask of a paraprofessional and the official pages that state them, naming the education route, any test and passing score, and the background check.
Every adult in a school helps keep children safe. If a child is in danger right now, call 911 (or your local emergency number) and get help at once.
State laws name the people who must report suspected child abuse or neglect, called mandated reporters. In many states school staff, including aides, are on that list. Your duty is to report what you saw or heard, not to prove it. Learn your state's law and your school's policy in your training: who you report to (often the state's child abuse reporting line or child protective services) and how fast. In some states, telling a teacher or principal does not take the place of your own report.
If a child tells you something: stay calm, listen, and thank them for telling you. Do not ask leading questions or investigate. Do not promise to keep it secret; say you will get help from people whose job is to keep kids safe. Write down the child's exact words, the date and time, and report the same day. Keep it private from everyone who does not need to know.
Childhelp's National Child Abuse Hotline, 1-800-422-4453, gives counseling and help any time; it is not itself a reporting line, but it can help you find where to report in your state.
Step by step:
- If the child is in danger now, call 911.
- Listen calmly; do not investigate or ask leading questions.
- Do not promise to keep it secret.
- Write down the child's exact words, the date and the time.
- Report the same day the way your state law and school policy say.
- Keep it private from everyone who does not need to know.
Words to know:
- Mandated reporter: a person the law requires to report suspected child abuse or neglect.
- Neglect: when a child's basic needs, like food, shelter, care or supervision, are not met.
- Child protective services (CPS): the state or county agency that looks into reports of child abuse and neglect.
- Leading question: a question that suggests the answer, like "Did your dad hit you?"
Official sources:
- Child Welfare Information Gateway: mandatory reporting of child abuse and neglect
- Child Welfare Information Gateway: how to report child abuse and neglect
- Child Welfare Information Gateway: state statutes search
- Childhelp National Child Abuse Hotline
Try it now: Final task: write your Paraprofessional Readiness Plan. Put in your state and district requirements with links, your route and study dates, your small-group activity from Lesson 4, and the safety steps from this lesson with your state's child abuse reporting number (look it up on the Child Welfare Information Gateway "how to report" page).
You can now say what to do when a child may be harmed, who you report to and when, and put your whole path to a paraprofessional job on paper.
How your final task is checked:
What we look at Not yet Meets Exceeds Requirements checked Requirements are guessed or come from an unofficial source. Lists the state and one district's education route, test and score (if any) and background check, with official links. Also compares two districts and notes pay or other steps such as training. Study plan No test date, or no plan for what to study. A real test date (or a route without a test) and one study focus per week. Includes scores from practice sets and the weak areas they showed. Small-group activity The activity does not match the teacher's goal, or gives answers first. Follows the goal, has practice items, two hints before answers, and a note to the teacher. Also plans a quick way to see which students need more help. Behavior and privacy Uses real student names or details, or plans to share them outside school staff. Uses made-up initials and says who may and may not see student information. Adds a calm, positive response to one behavior that follows a student's plan. Safety steps Missing the emergency step, promises secrecy, or plans to investigate. Lists the steps in order with the state's reporting number and the same-day timing. Notes what the school's own policy adds, after asking the school or reading it. To pass: Meets or Exceeds on every row. If a row is Not yet, fix that part and try again.

check.q: A child tells you an adult at home hurts them and asks you not to tell. What do you say?
options: "Are you sure? That doesn't sound true."
"Thank you for telling me. I need to tell people whose job is to keep you safe."
"Tell me every detail so I can decide."
check.why: You never promise secrecy, and you don't question or judge; you get help from the right people.

check.q: When should a mandated reporter report a concern?
options: After talking to the family first
At the end of the school year
The same day, the way state law and school policy say
check.why: You report what you saw or heard, quickly; proving it is CPS's or the police's job.
